Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
It reinforces our commitment to inclusive connectivity across our footprint. In November, our acquisition of a strategic stake in South Africa's fiber business, MAZIV, received ICASA's final approval. In fiber to the home, MAZIV's footprint exceeds 2.8 million homes, representing market leadership. The business also has scale in fiber to the business and fiber to the tower. With the injection of cash and assets from Vodacom, this transaction unlocks an opportunity to accelerate fiber deployment in South Africa and expand access to high-quality connectivity, particularly in historically underserviced communities.
In December, we announced an agreement to acquire an additional 20% stake in Safaricom. The acquisition, which is subject to certain conditions precedent and regulatory approvals, will result in the consolidation of Safaricom and cement the group's communication and fintech leadership in Africa.
For example, if we use our half-year numbers to September 2025 and extrapolate the combined revenues of Safaricom and Vodacom, we'll exceed ZAR 220 billion, with financial services making up 22% of service revenue. We remain on track to close this transformational deal in the current quarter. From a performance perspective, we delivered another excellent quarter. The group's commercial momentum and more stable macro backdrop gives us confidence in our medium-term growth trajectory and bodes well for the group's financial performance for our full-year results.
For Q3, at a group level, revenue was ZAR 43.9 billion, up 11%. Group service revenue grew 2.7% in rands and was up 13.6% on a normalized basis, tracking favorably against our medium-term targets. The quarter showcased another excellent performance from Egypt, with a stable performance in South Africa and further improvement in our international business.
I was particularly pleased with our performance in Beyond Mobile and, specifically, financial services. Beyond Mobile services reached 22.9% of group service revenue, up from 21.4% in Q3 of the prior year. Our financial service business, which is the largest component of Beyond Mobile, was up 24.7% in rands to ZAR 4.5 billion. On a normalized basis, financial service growth accelerated to 26.1%, with all our geographies improving from Q2. We remain Africa's leading financial services operator, with $501 billion of transactions processed through our mobile money platforms over the last 12 months, including Safaricom.
This represents an impressive $1.4 billion every day. Shifting focus to South Africa, service revenue grew 1.4% to ZAR 16.4 billion, supported by strong performance in the consumer contract segment and Beyond Mobile services.
Mobile contract revenue was 2.6%, and we expect our 1 February price ups to accelerate this trend into the final quarter. In prepaid, we left a strong comparison in the prior year and reported a decline of 3.6%. As mentioned, our Beyond Mobile numbers were good, with financial services up 8.4%, fixed up 7.9%, and some good project wins in IoT, pushing up IoT revenue by 33.9%. The revenue numbers for the quarter were not impacted by the MAZIV transaction. MAZIV is an associate and included in our books from 1 December 2025.
The transaction is not expected to have a material effect on the group's headline earnings for financial year 2026. Egypt delivered another excellent performance. In rand terms, Egypt's revenue was ZAR 11.1 billion and grew 43.7% in rands. Service revenue in local currency was up 39.7%, contributing 27.5% of the group result.
The growth was broad-based, with strong growth in consumer mobile, fixed business, and Vodafone Cash. Vodafone Cash revenue grew 59.4% to ZAR 926 million and increased its contribution to 9.7% of Egypt's service revenue. Financial service customers were up 28.9% to 13.5 million. For Q4, we expect service revenue growth to trend into the 20s as the business laps the 30% price increases from December 2024. Now, switching to our international business, the positive momentum continues. Reported service revenue was ZAR 8.8 billion, up 12.6%, making up 25.5% of the group.
Normalized service revenue was 15.4%, accelerating from the Q2 growth of 14.2%. The acceleration reflected an improvement in DRC and Mozambique. In DRC, we grew service revenue 16.3% in US dollars, supported by data and M-PESA.
Service revenue in Mozambique was up 7% in local currency, making a clear improvement from prior quarters. Tanzania continued to deliver excellent growth of 19.8% in shillings, while Lesotho was up 10.8%. M-PESA revenue was ZAR 2.6 billion, up 22.1%. Our fourth business segment is Safaricom. The results for the Safaricom group are disclosed on a biannual basis and therefore not included in the quarterly update. However, Safaricom did provide a market update on Ethiopia. The business is scaling at a good pace. Customers reached 12.2 million, up from 7.1 million a year ago.
Local currency service revenue growth in Ethiopia more than doubled. In December, we revised mobile data and voice pricing structures to support the long-term sustainability and quality of our services. The adjustments reflected evolving cost dynamics across the business, including continued investment in network expansion and modernization, as well as broader macroeconomic factors and currency movements.
This change to pricing structures follows constructive engagement with the government and regulator. That concludes my review. Raisibe and I are now ready to answer any questions you may have.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Thank you, Shamil. Our first few questions are from Prashendran of 36ONE. I'll take the first two of them, and then perhaps, Shamil, you can take the third one. The first question is just around the devices in South Africa, noting that 5G devices are up, growing nicely year-on-year. The question being, how many 3G and 2G devices do we still have on the network, and what are the trends there? I'll come back to that in a second.
The second question is, within the data traffic growth of 32.3%, is that for prepaid or postpaid or for both? And then the third question for you, Shamil, is, how much has voice revenue declined in the quarter in South Africa? So Prashendran, maybe just kicking off with the handset side of the question.
We've got still around 6 million 2G handsets on the network, but those are falling around 10% year-on-year at the moment. The biggest decline we're seeing across the base is on 3G. We're at about 2.4 million handsets now, and that's down around 40% year-on-year, clearly being compensated for by the 4G and 5G device growth. Then in terms of the data traffic question, actually, that 32% is reasonably even across both prepaid and contract, contract with slightly faster growth in the quarter.
But if we look at the quarter-on-quarter change from the last quarter to the Q3, the Q2 to the Q3, it's prepaid that really accelerated a bit. Shamil, to you on the voice revenue decline.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So the voice revenue decline is about -13% for the quarter.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Okay. Madhvi from HSBC.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Just to also specify that it's now about 30% of our service revenue.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Madhvi from HSBC has a number of questions, so if I can ask you to take out your pens and pencils. The first one is around the Safaricom stake and stake sale. He's asking about the prospects for the government's holding going forward, whether that could go to zero over time, and the potential that could have for an adverse regulatory climate. So what assurances do we have in place regarding government's continued investment in Safaricom?
The separate question on South Africa: Madhvi noting that with prepaid still weak, are we now seeing pressure in the contract side as well? So maybe a little bit of color around contract. And within prepaid, is the pressure really coming from WhatsApp bundles of Telkom and the competition from MVNOs? How should we think about that?
The final question, and I appreciate a lot from Madhvi, but they're also asked by several others, is just one on Egypt, is around sorry, is one around Egypt, and that's asking, are there any scope for price ups in Egypt in the short run?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Okay. So maybe firstly, on the Safaricom part, in terms of the government holding, I think government's very, very, very clear that they intend holding the 20% for the foreseeable future. And you don't need to take my word for it. You just need to look at the parliamentary transcripts on it. It's quite emotional for government even having sold down a percentage. But they see Safaricom as a strategic investment and have every intention of holding that for a very long time, if not forever.
Secondly, so on the second question on prepaid, is there contract pressure? No. So on contract, essentially, a little bit of, I would say, enterprise is flattish. Consumer is growing more than 5%, and that's why you've got a result of just over 2.6% for the contract segment. So contract continues to grow, consumer contract continues to grow strongly.
Enterprise has always got a little bit of pricing, and I think one of the big things there is not that we're losing customers. Customers are still growing. The big issue's been some of the legacy stuff. So I'll give an example. Universities now deciding to scale down on the bundles that they were giving students, that type of thing. So you'll get some of those things that people have exited, but a lot of that would be in the base going forward. In prepaid, where's the pressure coming from? I mentioned the -13% on voice. That's probably your biggest pressure point that you're faced with.
And then the data, revenue growth has not been as strong as we would have previously liked. The traffic is strong, but remember, we've gone through repricing, and that's where it's coming from.
We see Q4 being a lot stronger, and then going into the new year, we see that turning to positive. Then basically, in Egypt, in terms of price ups, we'll always strive for price ups, and we'll always have conversations around it. But I think it becomes price ups are more of an issue because the price floors and the regulated floor environment creates a very healthy growth. If there's a big currency movement, price ups become more important.
And in that context, as we've shown, the regulatory authorities are willing to consider and listen to that based on if inflation/currency has basically had a bigger movement, then they would be open up to they'd be open to those discussions.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
One small build on the business side of South Africa. So if you look at the overall Vodacom Business result, we are growing 6.7%. What we're doing well at the moment is where we're asking a little bit of pressure in mobile and at an account level. We're seeing good traction with our Beyond Mobile services, particularly areas like cloud, IoT, and fixed. Shifting gear to Jonathan from Prescient. He wanted a little bit of color around the competitive intensity or the competitive landscape in South African prepaid. Maybe you can just reiterate or clarify your point around the growth outlook.
He's just asking, when can we return to growth in prepaid? Separate to that, Jonathan's asking for some color around the drivers for the strong other service revenue line, which grew 23% in the quarter.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Okay. On prepaid, essentially, so firstly, big picture. From a competitive perspective, very much the same as Q3, except what we did was we repriced a lot of our bundles or what we call our LTE bundles to make sure that we were competitive. We took pricing from being below the line to above the line and provided customers with more clear, simple offers. And that's worked quite nicely for us. Of course, we were betting against a strong quarter last year because of the Two-Pot system and so on.
So when we look at the quarter-on-quarter performance and we look at all the different metrics, I think strong performance there. The residual issue, of course, is voice. And so basically, voice is under pressure, and we're trying to reduce the decline by offering things like unlimited voice and these type of things and bundles and so on.
But also, when you move from out-of-bundle to in-bundle, you see a temporary decline because you take that hit, but you've saved that revenue for longer. So those are kind of transformations that we're going. So we're busy with a, I'd say, there's a bit of a price transformation happening. We see that stepping down, the -3.6 being lower or much lower in Q4. And in Q1, we see it turning back into positive.
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
In terms of the question about the other services, so the main driver is IoT, but noting that those are contracts that in some cases are short-term and they're lumpy, but the main growth of the 23% was driven by that.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Nadim from Standard Bank is staying in South Africa, and I just wanted to know if the summer campaign met our expectations and any sense of what we thought actually worked well and what didn't in the period. Nadim, I see you had a question on the SA voice revenue decline in Q3. I think we've already nailed that one. So Shamil, maybe just a little bit on the summer campaign.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So, on the summer campaign, very much met our expectations. I mean, what we were trying to do is, of course, do some of the price transformation and offset it with the, let's say, increase in traffic, increase of utilization, increase of bundle purchases, and so on during the summer campaign, and rewarding that behavior with VodaBucks and so on. And then also, so we've seen that play out quite nicely during the quarter.
What we also wanted to do was more increase our direct purchasing on VodaPay and the number of users and so on on digital. And all of that has turned out very well, and we've exceeded our expectations in that regard. So we're quite happy with the performance that we're seeing.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Rohit from Citi, maybe this one's for you, Raisibe, the first one. Just wanted a bit of color around the South African EBITDA margin trend in the second half of the year and, I guess, calling out that previous guidance we had of around mid-single-digit growth in South Africa. Is that possible? He had a separate question then that I guess we can take between Shamil and myself around the data traffic growth in Egypt. What's driving that? And are you seeing higher data usage from 5G adoption in Egypt? But perhaps, Raisibe, you can kick off with the EBITDA.
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So we see EBITDA stable and a better outcome compared to the first half, in part as we have seen the revenue trends picking up, especially in the prepaid space, and also boosted by the price increase. Our cost efficiency programs continue, and we're quite confident that it will deliver. So that should create a stable margin, EBITDA margin, and also EBITDA growth.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
So on Egypt, what we're seeing is, of course, a 25% increase in traffic. So very happy with that. Coupled with an 8.9% growth in data customers. So that's helped to accelerate data revenue. What's driving it is investment. We see a payback of under a year when we basically put in new sites in Egypt. So it's driven by additional coverage on the one side, but mainly it's driven by additional 5G coverage that we've now launched. And given the high smartphone penetration in Egypt, that's picking up quite nicely.
But it's also alleviating pressure on the 4G network, which is then allowing us to monetize faster there. The other thing that we do very well in Egypt, which we've now basically taken as best practice across the group, is monitoring what we call the busy hour.
So normally, when you build a network, you build for you dimension the network for busy hour. We built a tool using AI that actually looks at multiple busy hours during the day and then determines and comes back with a recommendation on where you should build or put the CapEx first so that you get immediate monetization of that. And that's now playing out into the different markets, also rolling out into the IB markets and so on, and is helping to make sure that the CapEx spend is even more targeted to generate more revenue faster.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
We're going to move to questions from Jono from Absa. He has a few, so pens at the ready, please. First one around the dynamic between data revenue growth in South Africa, prepaid data revenue growth of 3%, and then the data traffic growth of around 30%. Are you going to keep the same level of promotional activity into Q4 and then into FY27? Second question around IoT. Is there scope for additional contract wins under the RT29 tender? So can this type of growth, I guess, continue?
Tanzania noting a slight slowdown quarter-over-quarter. Was this across both GSM and fintech or skewed to one side or the other? Or maybe just a little bit of color around why TZ slowed a little?
And then finally, around the Safaricom transaction, Jono is noting that the East African competition authorities have penciled in a submission date for 16 February. Given this is the biggest deal they've looked at, is there a risk they could delay the transaction approval into financial year 2027?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So maybe just to start off with on the data revenue growth. So effectively, what we're seeing is that, as you can see, the traffic growth has been very strong. Now, normally, we get a much better growth coming through in terms of the monetization than the 3% that you saw in the quarter. And the reason for that is the repricing that we went through in terms of taking stuff from below the line, making it more visible above the line. That helped us to grow customers.
It helped us to consolidate spend from various customers into single SIMs and so on. So we're quite happy with what it is. Of course, summer is summer, so when you step into the next phase, you don't run promotions continuously.
So yes, some of the promotions will step down, and then, of course, we'll run other lesser promotions that are not, let's call it, summer promotions. But you'll see, as that transformation happens and people are spending more, you'll also see that the data absolute revenue growth will accelerate. So that's what we're expecting, is that the data revenue growth, the traffic, we think will stay high, but we think we'll see a better monetization of the data growth as we were seeing before we went through this repricing, transparent stuff that we did.
And so I think let's just say we're quite happy that the strategy and the plan that we've put in place will work in terms of taking prepaid back to growth. The growth rates for next year, we're looking at just slightly above inflation-type growth for South Africa while we're doing that last bit of transformation.
The broader group will be within the targets that we've communicated in our growth targets in service revenue and EBITDA. In terms of IoT, yes, definitely more opportunities to win on RT29. We're seeing a lot of focus on people moving to prepaid electricity meters and so on. And also, the work that we've done in water and that we continue to do, work that we continue to do with our water tower and so on in the IoT segment is we're starting to get more and more wins in that respect, so we'll continue to push.
It can be, to Raisibe's point earlier, it can be a bit lumpy from time to time because it takes a while sometimes to win some of these. And then you've got the short-term revenue, and then you've got, of course, the ongoing part of that as well.
In Tanzania, the slowdown is very much to do with elections and the disruptions that happened in that market. You saw an entire market slowdown during that period. Once that period finished into December, you basically saw revenue growth accelerate back to the previous levels that we were experiencing. Then in terms of the approvals, we think, I mean, of course, things can take longer than you expect, but we don't see big delays in terms of the transaction. We're still hopeful that we'll be able to close it before the end of March.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
One quick follow-up from Jono before we move on to the next set of questions. I just wanted to know if there's any material or noticeable changes in the competitive environment in South Africa since we last spoke in November?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
No, not really. I mean, I'd say very much the same. We're seeing MVNOs come and go at a rapid pace, so that's been quite interesting. And some, I'm told, very, very little uptake. So that's been quite interesting. No big changes in pricing. Of course, everybody had their summer promos and their summer offers and so on, but I don't think there's been any massive changes. We've seen postpaid changes and postpaid price-ups from almost everyone, so that's gone through. And yeah, so not much more. No real aggression or anything of that sort.
And of course, I mean, one of the big things would be just kind of we've gone through that repricing part, which, as I said previously, was caused by some changes in pricing, not so much from the MVNOs but really, I would say, led by MTN.
But we've done our own transparent transformations and so on, and we've seen them stopping some of those promotions as well.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
You're going to shift to Myron from BofA. Perhaps the first question for you, Raisibe. He's asking around the Safaricom debt or I suspect this is around the acquisition debt, when it could become tax-deductible or if it could become tax-deductible. There is a clarification around the split between consumer and enterprise contract in South Africa, so I'll perhaps help with that in terms of revenues. Third one, Shamil, for you. Have the authorities now said no to further price-ups in Egypt? So have we got a definitive no?
And related to that, why would Egypt service revenue grow in the '20s in Q4 despite decent customer growth and data usage? The final question he has, again, perhaps for you, Shamil, is around the amount of prepaid revenue we're now being purchased through VodaPay. So Raisibe, to you on the Safaricom debt, acquisition debt?
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So the debt is non-tax-deductible, as in the term debt. The approach that we have taken is that we will look at opportunities for refinancing, as we have done previously with the Egypt transaction where we managed to refinance part of the bundle with the preferences. So the good thing is that we are already in discussions with the banks in terms of taking the first part of the Safaricom transaction into prefs. You'd appreciate the size of the transaction, that we can't go into preferences for the whole packet all in one go.
So we will start the process as we progress. The other angle is that for all our non-tax-deductible debt, we prioritize in terms of repayment. And previously, we did repay some of the debt. So that is the approach that we'll continue to take in this case.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
I'll take the revenue split in South Africa postpaid between consumer and enterprise. It's not quite 50/50. It is skewed to the contract segment, the consumer contract segment, excuse me. So to get the math to work, consumer contract, as Shamil said, growing 5% to 6%, and enterprise is in a small decline. That's how we square the circle there. Shamil, did you want to take the one around price-ups in Egypt?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So the price-ups in Egypt, effectively, there's no imminent price-up coming. But have they said no? No, they haven't said no. So essentially, it's a discussion that we always have, and you have to go with a motivation of the impact and how inflation has impacted you and these types of things. So let's just say you've got to have very good reasoning. I mean, if you're coming with a 3, 4, or 5% impact, they're not going to jump over the table and put a price up. So you need to it's got to be where it's really where let's say the inflationary pressures have affected the business or rather the industry.
So I mean, so that's where we are at the moment. Why 20%? Well, effectively, I mean, if you look at your traffic growth, why it's not 20%.
It's in the 20s, just to be clear. Basically, what that means, if you look at your traffic remember what I've always said? Traffic times rate. Rate is steady. Traffic converts into revenue. So previously, if you think about it, traffic, 25%, rate steady, you should have seen 25% growth, okay? Let's say you've got a few years. Example. Then if you put the price up on top of that, that's what took you to the 39% growth. So if you don't have that, traffic times rate will give you the growth rate for Egypt. So if your traffic is growing in the 20s, your revenue will grow in the 20s.
In terms of how much airtime is being purchased through VodaPay, we're at about 12%, and that's growing all the time. So it's notching up slowly.
Remember, we were at 3% for the better part of, sure, 10, 15 years. So actually, it's been very good in terms of, in the last year, 18 months, we've more than tripled the amount of airtime we're selling directly.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Prashendran from 36ONE has a follow-up. I can probably take this one. Let's see how it goes. With the massive transaction finalized on 1 December, how much fixed-line revenue in South Africa moved from the top line to the share of profits and associate? Because we are still reporting growth in South Africa. So Prashendran, there's no material impact on revenue. We still retain the relationship with the customer as effectively an ISP. What will obviously change is the margin profile of that revenue going forward as you move from the owner of the infrastructure to the reseller of that infrastructure.
Madhvi from HSBC had a follow-up. Shamil, how do we see the new data regulations in South Africa impacting Vodacom, both in terms of bundle expiry, and data transfer rules?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So on the data regulations, so firstly, I think the good part is that all the shorter-term bundles, which are about 80% of what the industry sells, are not affected. So that has been purely excluded. There are certain things that we're not happy with. The rollover on normal bundles, all of that, that's fine. The issue comes in specifically on FWA. So that part, we will go back to the, so the choices are simple. Put the price up to compensate, or they need to remove it.
So the regulators overstretch their hand a bit in terms of it because, as an example, they also look after broadcasting, but they don't tell MultiChoice what to include in their bundles. So that's the piece that we will have a discussion with them because it doesn't come into effect immediately.
So we will both as an industry and as Vodacom have a discussion with them in terms of the impacts of that and what does that mean. Because the last thing you want to do is to have to compensate by putting the price up. From the telco perspective, you'd have to do that to manage the impact and to make sure that it doesn't have a big impact on or a big impact on your numbers.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Anoop, yeah.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
But it's only for a small portion of basically the numbers. And that, we think, we'll have a conversation because I think you can't roll over a 500 GB bundle. It's a simple logic.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Anoop from Moon Capital had a question around the margin outlook for Egypt without further price increases. Raisibe, maybe that's one for you?
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. I mean, Egypt at half-year was roughly 44%. And that is the kind of level that we still expect. So although, I mean, the normal really bracket of 42, the levels where we are at 44 is still quite a strong margin, 46%. So that is still the level that you are comfortable with. But yeah, I mean, the absence of a price increase is not something that we are particularly concerned about. Egypt is still having some momentum to grow. And we expect that while service revenue will moderate, but inflation is also moderated, and therefore, their costs are well, well controlled. So they will still be able to maintain some margin.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
I've got a question from Robert of Deutsche Bank. He notes that the South African 10-year yield has continued to fall now to its lowest level in a decade, which is good news for all of us. Does this change how we think about our overall leverage profile? And is there any perhaps even anecdotal evidence of improving confidence for B2B customers with regard to new ICT projects in South Africa? So maybe, Raisibe, you can lead with that one. And then for Safaricom, just to clarify, Robert, just on the Safaricom deal, the approval process is moving along, and yes, we do expect at this point still to close in this calendar quarter, Q1.
Raisibe Morathi
CFO, Vodacom Group Limited
So I mean, good macros definitely welcome, but we all know that these kind of things come and go. So what we have done now, we continue to pay off debt, prioritize on the basis of expensive debt, being how it is priced as well as non-tax deductibility, converting to prefs, and we'll continue that journey. Now, while the deleverage is part of our strategy, we have just currently taken new debt. We've done preferences to finance the massive acquisition, and we will soon also pick up the debt relating to the Safaricom transaction. So the basket keeps on changing, and our focus is optimization so that our overall cost of funding is controllable.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
Anything to add on the B2B environment or South Africa more broadly?
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. I think the more positivity we can get, exchange rates improving, and so on. We need to see that converting into stronger GDP growth. The outlook looks very positive. And so I think that will stand us in good stead as we go into the new year. So inflation is much lower than before. So I think we're going into a better environment, interest rates coming down. So yeah, the trajectory for South Africa looks a lot more positive, coming off the gray list, the upgrade in terms from the rating agencies. So I think all in all, a very positive outlook for SA going forward.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
A question from Jonathan of Prescient is asking around our strategy to convert those remaining 6 million 2G customers in South Africa to 4G or 5G handsets and avoid churn within the space. Obviously, Jonathan, just to note, within that 6 million, there will be a whack of IoT devices.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Yeah. So look, I think there's a couple of things that we're doing. One is the industry is now making sure we can—we've got a clear recommendation from the industry forum to government, and we've been having long conversations with them about stopping the import of 2G devices outside of the IoT devices, 2G and 3G for that matter. We want to—actually, prioritizing 3G is even more important to us than the 2G part, but we have to move the 2G and 3G customers off. So what we've done is a couple of things.
Firstly, and you'll see that across the group in terms of the acceleration of—we've added more than 15 million data customers in the nine months to date this year. So we've beaten all our targets. And what we're doing is device financing, both ourselves and third parties.
So things like FoneYam from PEP, plus our own services, plus third-party services, all of that helps to basically reduce the number of 2G, 3G devices in the network. Secondly, price points. We're now at $25 a smartphone, but we've also got $15 cloud-based phones. Consumers are taking it up, but they prefer nicer phones. So they prefer actually, when you put the $15 and the $25 next to each other, they take the $25. So that's the one part that we're pushing, especially if they're paying off the device. So that, we're definitely pushing.
And then we deliberate in terms of trying to move certain customers and putting deliberate offers to them specifically on 2G to 4G and 3G to 4G migrations. So there's a clear plan in terms of how we do it coupled with if you stop the inflow, basically, the phones will fall off quicker.
[Analyst] (Vodacom Group Limited)
Analyst, Vodacom Group Limited
We have a follow-up question from Jono from Absa. He's asking if we're able to share what proportion of our traffic in South Africa is out-of-bundle for prepaid. Jono, I don't have that number in front of me, but just from a data revenue perspective for prepaid, the out-of-bundle, well, the overall out-of-bundle spend is immaterial in the context of overall South Africa. It's very low single digits of what is now out-of-bundle data revenue. So hopefully, that still addresses the question you had. Okay. That brings us to the end of the Q&A. I don't have any more questions, so we'll hand back to you, Shamil, for some quick closing comments.
Shameel Joosub
CEO, Vodacom Group Limited
Thank you. I mean, we're very pleased with the set of results, and we look forward to engaging with you on the investor calls and so on. Thank you for joining us today. And if you have any questions, please reach out to our investor relations team. Enjoy the rest of your day. Thank you.

content.text:
Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Before moving to Q&A, I will briefly provide an update on our transformation progress and financial performance. I want to specifically talk you through our operational execution in H1 in Germany and the UK. In Germany, our turnaround continues, and in the UK, we are now driving the integration of Vodafone and Three, both of which remain top priorities. First, a quick recap on our position as a group. As you know, over the past 2.5 years, we have changed both where we operate and how we operate. In the last 6 months, we have completed the reshaping of the group that I announced in May 2023. We have completed the merger of Vodafone and Three in the UK and the acquisition of Telekom Romania's assets.
All of Vodafone's operations are now in a strong position at scale in all our markets, and importantly, all these markets have sustainable structures. Our capital structure has also been reset, with appropriate investment levels, a stronger balance sheet, and over EUR 5 billion returned to shareholders via buybacks and dividends over the last 18 months, with a further EUR 1 billion of buybacks to come over the next 6 months. Most importantly, we have also delivered a step change in our operational transformation. Whilst we still have more to do in our drive to operational excellence, we have boosted customer satisfaction, we have simplified our operations, and powered growth beyond traditional connectivity by expanding our digital and financial services. Now, mentioning growth leads me on well to our financial results. We performed well in H1 in line with our expectations.
Our group service revenue growth has accelerated to 5.8% in Q2, supported by growth across Europe and Africa. On the profitability front, group EBITDA grew by 6.8% in H1, with nearly all our markets posting EBITDA growth. With this solid performance across the group and a positive outlook, we have confirmed today that we now expect to close the year at the upper end of the growth guidance that we set out in May. Alongside solid financial results, we have also made good operational progress in Germany and the UK. Our two largest markets have different starting points and different competitive landscapes, but both markets are demonstrating the impact of our strategic priorities: customer, simplicity, and growth. Taking each market in turn. Germany is the largest telecom market in Europe, and we operate at scale across both mobile and fixed.
In mobile, our 5G Standalone network covers over 90% of the population and now serves over 40 million customers, including 1&1, as well as almost 60 million IoT SIMs. On fixed broadband, we can offer gigabit connectivity to 3 out of 4 German households, more than any other operator in the country. Our gigabit broadband reach has indeed continued to expand during the quarter. We are now marketing OXG fiber to 1 million homes. Our brand is strong, customer satisfaction in Germany has stepped up in the last 2 years. We have simplified customer journeys. We have introduced GenAI in customer care across chatbots and agent assistance, our improvements across all call center KPIs are being recognized by independent testers. In terms of growth, we have followed a disciplined execution focused on value.
We have introduced new propositions in mobile, driving differentiation and upselling, and we have continued to increase front book ARPUs in fixed. We also continue to expand our capabilities to satisfy the growing demand for digital services. Just two weeks ago, we announced the acquisition of an established cloud service specialist active across Germany and Europe. Looking at Germany as a whole, we are well-positioned to drive structural growth as we have the right assets and the right team in place. A team that is fully focused on becoming the market leader in customer experience, a one-stop shop provider for fixed, mobile, and TV, and a trusted B2B partner of choice. Now on to the UK.
We are the largest mobile operator in the country, serving almost 30 million mobile customers, and we are also the fastest-growing broadband provider with the largest gigabit footprint of any operator, just like in Germany, as we are able to sell fiber to about 22 million UK households. Vodafone UK is already the market leader in customer satisfaction, and we are now extending our customer experience standards to Three customers. All of our customers are set to benefit from our GBP 11 billion network investment as we build the best-in-class 5G network for the UK. We have made a very fast start. Independent tests are already confirming noticeably better speeds and coverage in less than 6 months. In terms of growth, as you know, we have good commercial momentum in the UK, which is now being supported by our cross-selling opportunities.
With Vodafone broadband offers now open to Three customers and FWA open to Vodafone customers. Our multi-brand approach is proving effective in making the most of the market demand opportunities. The combination of these revenue synergies with our GBP 700 million cost and CapEx synergies gives us a strong growth trajectory in the UK. We will leverage our unique assets in the market to extend our customer experience leadership, monetize our improved mobile network quality, and continue to drive fixed service growth. This is just our two largest markets. We hold leadership positions across our African markets. Where yesterday the team reported another strong set of results in line with their medium-term double-digit EBITDA growth guidance. We are excited about the future in Africa as it combines structural opportunities across all our services from core connectivity to financial services to B2B. Coming back to group in closing.
Our objectives continue to be the same, to improve our customer experience across our markets, further simplify our business, and deliver sustainable cash flow growth in FY26 and beyond. The turnaround of Germany, the UK integration, and our strong positions in growing markets across Europe and Africa all give me confidence in our growth outlook. With the reshaping of the group behind us, now is the right time to deliver on our ambition to grow our dividend over time. We announced today that we are moving to a progressive dividend policy. Now Luka and I are looking forward to your questions.
Thank you, Margherita. As a reminder, please only pose one question to give all analysts a chance to speak. The first question this morning comes from Maurice Patrick at Barclays. Maurice, please go ahead.
Yeah. Hi, guys. Hope you can hear me fine. If I could ask a little bit about the EBITDA run rate for the H2 and also next year. You've delivered 6.8% organic year-on-year growth. You tightened the guidance towards the upper end of the range. I think if I look at the FY guidance, it implies 4% or 5% growth for the FY. Your guidance even at the high end seems to imply a slowdown versus the H1, despite Germany probably having easier comps as you exit the MDU drag. I know you called out higher stack in the UK, for example.
It's probably a bit early to talk about FY27, if you could give us some indications of some of those building blocks, that'd be very helpful. Thank you.
Sure. Luka, all over to you.
Excellent. Well, first of all, of course, we are very, very pleased with our performance in H1 on the EBITDA front. This was really a combination of very strong emerging markets growth, the UK doing very well, and then Germany improving as well over the last year, given that the MDU impact is now dissipating and we had the benefit of wholesale. If you look forward to H2, yes, our outlook at the high end of the range implies a slowdown. There are three factors that I would call out for that.
On the positive front, we absolutely expect Germany to continue to improve in H2, because we have zero MDU impact, and we will reach the full run rate of our wholesale migration of 1&1 this quarter. From Q4, we will then be at full run rate, just standing at around 11 million. We're almost done with the migration there. This will help of course. On the flip side, first of all, we continue to expect that our emerging markets growth contribution will trend down given that inflation moderates. You have seen some of that already in H1. I think that trend can be expected to continue.
Also the UK, which had a very good H1, will see a slowdown in EBITDA growth, first, because, I know I've talked about that already on the last earnings, but there should be a slowdown in top line growth, in particular in Q3, as we're facing very tough compares, in particular in our B2B business, where we had a positive one-off last year. Which should then sequentially increase and improve going into Q4 and beyond into FY27, but it will dampen the performance.
We also had some phasing impacts in the strong performance in H1. In the sense that the marketing expenses that are planned for this fiscal year in the UK are more back-end loaded to H2. If you pair that up with the emerging market slowdown that's driving the expectations. Now, FY27 is in particular for me very far out. Obviously, I am sure Margherita and Pilar will be back to give you a precise outlook going into FY27. From my perspective, perhaps just some high level puts and takes.
First of all, we would expect the UK to be a very positive contributor and have a strong EBITDA performance, based on the fact that we expect for the first time more sizable synergies from the merger coming together. For this year, there was really basically no contribution from synergies, but it will start to step up in the next year. In Germany, we will face puts and takes. Obviously, in H1, the benefit from the MDUs being fully out of the numbers, and in Q1, still a ramp-up effect from the wholesale migrations. For the remainder of the year, they will be out of the numbers in terms of a year-over-year help.
We will have to see what, you know, the market conditions do, to see what that means for the German performance. Also in FY27, I would continue to see a year-over-year challenge from an emerging markets growth perspective. On the positive note, I think what we are seeing is that the mix in our EBITDA contribution continues to shift back more favorably to Europe now, in the balance between emerging markets and Europe. That obviously drives also good predictability, which should be a net positive.
Thank you.
Thank you. The next question this morning comes from Akhil Dattani at JPMorgan. Akhil, please go ahead.
Hi. Good morning. Thanks for taking the question. I've got a question around Germany, just to unpack a bit of what you mentioned, Margherita, around the turnaround initiative that you've taken so far and how we see the fruits of that bearing into the numbers. You talked us through a lot of different things that you've done in Germany. If we look at the moment and we strip out the MDU effect and the 1&1 impact, the German revenue trends are still declining 2% to 3%. I'd love to understand what you think it takes and the timeline to see the underlying momentum starting to improve. If we layer onto that the scaling effect of 1&1, how should we think about the H2 outlook for Germany for revenue and EBITDA? Thanks a lot.
I will maybe ask Luca to take the last part of your question on one-on-one, and then I'll talk to the actions that we are taking. We seem to have a mic to fix. Apologies for the
I hope I was still able to be heard in my first answer.
Yes, you were. Please go ahead, Luka.
Thank you.
Thank you.
1&1 first.
Okay. Sure. First of all, in terms of our expectations for Germany, overall, we certainly expect that Germany will continue to grow in the H2 year. The wholesale support will obviously be a factor in that. I would also expect that towards the end of the year, our B2B performance will start to move upwards because we had very good success of contracting new digital services business. That always takes a while to come into the numbers, but that should be helping also the year-end performance there.
In terms of the impact that it has had, I really prefer always to talk about wholesale as a whole, because in conjunction with the 1&1 win, so to say, we had also then a subsequent loss of another smaller MVNO, Lyca, which went the other way around. If you make the math out of those, the contribution of both in the quarter was just above EUR 80 million as a whole. In H2, we would expect that the contribution from 1&1 will also be around EUR 100 million. In Q4, we are lapping then the loss of Lyca.
Those are kind of the puts and takes to take into account in terms of wholesale momentum.
In terms of underlying performance, if we exclude wholesale, Akhil, you are absolutely right. It's broadly stable. If I look at the H2 of the year, you shouldn't expect to see big step-ups Q on Q. Over time, the actions I was referring to in my introduction, which are all speaking to the long-term health of the business, will actually support our top line performance. It's a bit early to talk about 2027, as Luka was mentioning before, because, I mean, also in Germany, we will obviously have to see what the environment will be, both from a macro and from a competitive perspective. Whilst we should expect the headwind in TV to continue, and equally, we don't have full control of the dynamics in mobile, the top line will benefit from these actions.
Let me maybe bring this to life a little bit. First of all, we have talked about customer experience improving. With customers experience improving, we are seeing churns reducing. It's coming through in our numbers. Clearly, the customer experience is improving because of the investments in our networks, because the changes to our approach to customer service. Overall, net-net, the NPS is going up. We are continuing to beat record levels for us in fixed and stepping up in mobile. In some sub-segments, we are now actually leading in the market. Clearly, there is more to do, but all this is playing in our numbers to churn. I talk to the work we are doing on ARPU and supporting value in the market. We're really focused there on all what is in our control, and this is going to again help us.
In fixed, you will have seen, for example, us gradually moving up front book ARPU in the last six months. The last moves were only three weeks ago, and we are seeing the benefits of that. In mobile, we are upselling. Finally, actually, Luka mentioned B2B. B2B is perhaps one of our biggest growth opportunities in Germany. We are investing in digital services. Again, you heard the Skaylink acquisition. It's growing double digit. We see this as supporting growth going forward. All this as a package is really the result of the actions we have taken supporting our long-term health of the business as we go into FY27.
Great. Thank you much.
Thank you. The next question this morning comes from Carl Murdock-Smith at Citigroup. Carl, please go ahead.
That's great. Thank you very much. I wanted to ask about the UK. You touched in the presentation on making a fast start on integration. Can you provide a bit more color on your early actions and synergy delivery? Also comment on in what ways the commercial performance in Q2, and revenue has been a bit better than the decline you had suggested we could expect when you spoke at last quarter's results. Thank you.
Maybe again, I will let Luka start with the outperformance on the revenue front, and then I will pick up on the integration.
Yeah, happy to. I mean, normally, CFOs don't like surprises, but in this case I will make an exception. Indeed, we saw obviously coming into the merger a combination of a slowdown in Three that we have discussed at our last earnings call. We had the underlying challenge in our own business, so to say, before the merger with the B2B managed services terminations that we had to fight against. That was underpinning, I would say, a cautious stance. If you take into account that the team, of course, was to be very busy on all of the integration steps.
I have to say the teams together and driving for very, very positive actions in terms of rolling out our base management practices to Three. Making early wins on the network, quality and improvement front with the sharing of spectrum, and now increasingly the activation of MOCN, which obviously is positive, in particular, also helping performance on the Three network. In that sense, we have seen a combination of improving churn trends, very good consumer performance, in particular in home broadband, which I think had the biggest net adds jump in the quarter that we have ever seen in a Q2 in the UK. Also initial cross-selling benefits and successes.
FWA was a very positive story for us. That in combination has outweighed the underlying decline in B2B legacy managed services to an extent that frankly was a bit better than what we would have expected. Very positive. I should perhaps add as a last point that the good actual current commercial trading performance was not only in consumer, but we had actually also a good performance in B2B. Not enough, of course, to change the trends from the managed services side for this year, but of course, encouraging if we move further beyond that.
Just a bit more color on the actions. I'd say, and reiterate, as Luka said, the team is doing a really great job. I think we are progressing at a pace that has not seen before in UK telcos in terms of bringing the two companies together. Just to give you a sense, we're only a few months in, and we are already completing the integration of the third levels in the organization. On networks and on other operations, what are the things we are seeing? On the network front, we talked in Q1 about higher speeds for Three customers, the whole customer base of Three, because of how we are using the spectrum together. I'd say Q2 was all about rolling out our Multi-Operator Core Network to allow customers to use seamlessly both networks.
You may remember me saying that we had a target of 8,000 sites upgraded for MOCN by year-end. Well, actually it will be, I think by tomorrow is the latest. We will get there this week. This obviously talks to the reduction of not spots for our base, you know that we are targeting a surface of 10 times the size of London, and it's actually really visible today. You don't need to take my word for it. Opensignal has already published a report saying it's noticeable and measurable. I can't wait to tell you more about this in the coming quarters as we will also see the customer reactions. It's a very strong pace. Operationally, beyond the networks and the teams coming together, what is also coming together really well now is what I would call our multi-brand strategy.
We now have a single team, for example, in consumer, managing across all our brands, and these brands allow us to cover all market needs and do this in a consistent, coherent way, is quite powerful. As Luka mentioned, we have been opening cross-selling, so that's obviously supporting our commercial momentum. We were already the market leader in growth in broadband. We are now offering our broadband offers to the whole Three base and the FWA offers to the Vodafone base. As you can see, almost the first things we are excited about at the moment are the revenue synergies. These come, of course, on top of the EUR 700 million cost and CapEx synergies that are, of course, part of our business case. Good momentum in the UK, and you will see this continuing ahead of us.
That's great. Thank you very much.
Thank you. The next question comes from Polo Tang at UBS. Polo, please go ahead.
Morning. Thank you for taking the question. It's a question on Germany. There are proposed changes to legislation that will make it easier for operators such as Deutsche Telekom to access MDUs and deploy fiber. What's your view on the impact of these potential changes? Can you also talk through the economics for the OXG fiber JV? From memory, it's about EUR 7 billion of CapEx to build a footprint to 7 million homes. Can you remind us what the equity injections that are required for the JV, and how should we think about the wholesale costs that the German unit has to pay to the OXG JV longer term? Thanks.
Thank you, Polo. I think I will take both sides of your questions, maybe starting from the draft Telco Act, which is being discussed in Germany. There are a lot of measures as part of this that are all geared towards simplifying and accelerating high-speed network builds in Germany, for example, by simplifying permits processes. This is actually really good. It's good for the fiber build-out. It's good for the 5G build-out. I think the government is really pushing in the right direction in the country. Now, as part of all the discussion going on, there are some elements, and you referred into the in-building wiring debate that we feel are unnecessary, and we're openly sharing what I would call our real-life insights on what's happening on the fiber building.
I think it's very clear to everyone that the bottleneck in fiber building in Germany has nothing to do with housing association and has more to do with other factors such as construction capacity limits. Beyond that, today, these are discussions. There is no draft law to really comment upon, but just to take your point. Even if all the discussions that are going on were translating into law for the reasons I've just described, actually, the impact is going to be just a marginal, maybe, acceleration of the fiber building towards the housing associations, and that will benefit all players in the market, including OXG. It's unclear whether this discussion will ever become a draft law, and it's unclear at this point when this draft law will become law.
Assuming it happens, if it happens at some point, in 2026, you need to keep in mind, and I'm going to the next part of your question, that by then, OXG will be already marketing anyway to millions of customers in the housing associations. Standing back, I don't see this as a major impact on whatever speculation is going on, definitely. The other point I would say is that actually if you take all the discussions that are going on in Germany across the German Telco Act and across the copper switch off, again, I think it's moving in the right direction overall, and it will be supportive for telecoms overall. You asked about OXG economics, I think. On the equity injections, these are very small.
I mean, obviously, Luka could add any detail, but I think we said this when we were setting up the JV because of the, I would call it self-financing over time. It's really at the margin in terms of equity requirements, very small. On the front of the wholesale costs and revenues, depending on which side of the equation you look at, I think I know that there has been some work going on trying to from an analytics perspective, get to this calculation. I think it's really important that you keep in mind that. Let me say there are three nuances to the calculations that maybe are worth sharing, and IR can help you sort of bringing them to life more precisely than I can do in a call.
The first point is that there is no commitment or obligation whatsoever for Vodafone cable customers to be migrated to fiber into OXG. That just is not there. The second aspect is that 20% of the OXG footprint will be actually outside the cable areas. Obviously, penetration into the OXG households will build over time. It will build during the 6 years of rollout, which are exactly planned as you are describing, but it will also obviously continue to build after that. This is very gradual, and I think brings to, I would say, a different conclusion than some of the calculations we have seen. I would let really the IR team to help you out on where to go. I would just say that we are really happy with the progress now with OXG.
You know that the first year and a half, obviously, were challenging to set things up. We have now already built to 350,000 households. We have opened the sales to 1 million households. We have connected the first customers. We have also opened wholesale. 1&1 and the regional operator are already connected. 3 million households are already, let's say, committed in the construction orders. We have more than 30 construction partners. I mean, it's a big building site across many, many cities in Germany, and we now look forward to see this coming through in our numbers.
Yeah. Just very quickly on the equity. In 3 years, the equity contribution and injection was just above EUR 70 million. It's really to underscore the point for Margherita, very, very small.
Thank you.
Thank you. The next question this morning comes from Emmet Kelly at Morgan Stanley. Emmet, please go ahead.
Yes. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for taking my question. My question yet again this quarter is on Vodafone Turkey. On my numbers, it represents, I think, almost half of the organic EBITDA growth that we've seen since last year. I guess most notable is the EBITDA margin uptick at your Turkish business. Could you talk a little bit about the top line trends you're seeing there and expect to see and on your cost management program, if you could say a few words on that. Thank you.
Perhaps I can take this, because indeed, I mean, Türkiye has been a tremendous success story in the last couple of years, not only in terms of the financial success, which has been clearly there. Just to give you some absolute numbers, which are perhaps not so easily visible. Just in the last 2 years, they have increased both EBITDA as well as cash flow by close to EUR 300 million each, which for the size of the business is obviously a tremendous improvement. That's in hard currency, so not in local currency.
While that growth, of course, inevitably, as we had already indicated, has started to come down because of the lowering in inflation, it's still significantly outperforming inflation and in absolute terms in EUR, has still been in mid-teens on the service revenue front in the last quarter and was more than 20% up in some hard currency for the H1. Where is this coming from? It's coming from a set of unique capabilities. Yes, the team has always been very prudent and forward-looking and leaning into the inflation environment by managing costs very successfully. There is more to it from my perspective. Türkiye is probably among the best digital capabilities that we have across the group.
They have a very high proportion of digital sales. They have a very agile base management model, like a very targeted micro segment related calls to provide them access to targeted upsell offerings, post-to-post migrations. The team has really built a machine there around the set of digital capabilities that are very unique and that we are partially exporting also to other countries, such as the loyalty app, for example, the Vodafone Happy, that we're now also rolling out in other countries. It's not only a story of cost-cutting and riding an inflation wave, not at all. It's actually based on a very proven and successful management model.
While I've shared before that, as we think forward, certainly, the inflationary trends will continue to recede and therefore growth may come down. I think, they have been, you know, increasing also their relative competitive position in the market. I think that based on the strength of the management team will certainly continue.
If I can just build on that, Emmet, for a second. Looking at the group as a whole, we are extremely proud of Turkey, I need to say we're equally happy about all our countries. We regularly publish in our reports, the service revenue growth ex Turkey, given the hyperinflation environment, you have seen this growing to 3% in the quarter. This is a reflection of the strength of the portfolio. We have Africa, of course, also growing strongly. Double-digit EBITDA growth, which is in line with our upgraded guidance there. Overall, taking on the opportunities in the UK that we have just described and the turnaround in Germany, where we have now turned the corner with the top line, obviously are looking forward to the profitability improvement.
All this taken in aggregate is, I would say, where we wanted to be through the group transformation. It's the reason why you hear us talking about an outlook of midterm free cash flow growth. Yeah. Every part of the group is contributing.
Super. Thank you very much.
Thank you. The next question this morning comes from Joshua Mills at BNP Paribas Exane. Joshua, please go ahead.
Hi, guys. Hope you can hear me, and thank you for the question. I wanted to come back to the UK market and focus on your FWA proposition in particular. Following the Three UK merger in a very strong spectrum position, you mentioned in your comments earlier that you are happy with how the FWA business is developing. Could you give us a bit more detail about the net adds on that business and what your longer-term ambition with FWA might be, how you balance that against the desire to grow on the fixed broadband base as well? Perhaps just one short clarification. When you have your FWA customers, are they included in your broadband numbers or your mobile customer numbers? Thanks.
Yeah.
I'll start from. I'll cover it all in one go. The net adds are in mobile because that's the supporting technology. If I'm not mistaken, it's 17,000 in the quarter. They have accelerated. Let me talk to you about how we look at FWA more broadly. It's obviously a great opportunity for us to leverage what I would describe as our overall asset superiority in the market. We have. I was talking earlier, the largest fiber footprint available to our customers with 22 million households. Obviously fiber in the UK is not everywhere yet. We will be offering FWA to all the population in the UK, thanks to the capabilities that we have today.
We see it as an opportunity because it allows us to bridge the time until fiber comes and maybe cover areas also where fiber may not come at all in the most rural areas. If fiber comes, it's great to get our customers first on FWA and then moving them on as the time progresses. We really see it as an opportunity in the market. As I said before, it's now open to everybody, whether they are in Three brands or ex-Three brands, ex-Vodafone brands. We look forward to see this support our growth.
Thank you. Now to the next question from David Wright at Bank of America Merrill Lynch. David, please go ahead. David, we cannot currently hear you.
Oh, sorry. I'm on the.
Okay.
I do apologize and apologize for no video, although, maybe not a bad thing. Just a technical question, I suspect just for yourself, Luca. Super straightforward. In H1, adjusted EBITDA, common functions was maybe a little, excuse me, surprisingly negative. It shows EUR -14 million. It's been running a fairly consistent clip of EUR 22 million, EUR 23 million in the last couple of halves. Just any explanation there and just how we should think about that full-year number and maybe even into 2027. That's it for me. Thank you.
It reminds me of the old days.
Yeah.
Because when I was CFO, that it was a recurring question. Ultimately. It's actually quite structured. Maybe you want to go through that.
Yeah. Exactly. If I go back in the history to Margherita's days, before I arrived, I think historically, common functions EBITDA was actually always negative. Then, in the last 2 years, it turned positive as a result of some of the M&A activity that was going on, which created one-time effects. Last year it was also helped through a quite sizable central provision release. That is obviously creating headwinds in the year-over-year. Structurally, from a go-forward perspective, should actually expect common functions EBITDA to rather be negative than neutral to positive.
The reason for that is just simply that the help from kind of the M&A transition to also above the line EBITDA recognition essentially is dissipating.
Just to come back to why it's been structurally negative. It's a very simple thing, David. It's because you know that our shared operations costs are paid for in the markets, but that's not the case for what we call corporate services. Just the HQ cost. I mean, if I take ourselves and the IR team supporting this call, right? This stay at the central EBITDA level, which is a cost, but don't see this as big movements.
Okay. Could I take that H1 number and just double it for the full year? Is that reasonable? You know.
I-
Just get a proxy.
Well, it's an area that, again, because we are talking about small numbers, can have variations.
Okay
We wouldn't be very specific at that level of detail, to be honest.
That's great. Thank you, guys.
Thank you. The next question this morning comes from James Ratzer at New Street Research. James, please go ahead.
Yes, thank you very much. Good morning, Margherita and Luka. We haven't yet had a question on the dividend, I think.
